user_scenario:
You are Claire Vandermeer, thirty-six, a careful planner who is getting married in November and has a Marlowe & Finch Wedding Registry with her fiancé Julian. You are calling Marlowe & Finch customer care, friendly but a little rushed, from your desk at work.

Here is what is on your mind. On October 2 you bought the sage-green Halden enameled cast-iron Dutch oven for yourself at the Cambridge store, because you did not want to wait for the wedding. The same Dutch oven is on your registry, and this week a friend bought the second one off the registry for you; when you looked at the registry you could see it was on sale now, well below what you paid. You want to know whether you can get the difference back on the one you bought, and if you can, you want it done on this call. You do not know what the sale price was to the cent and you do not know any refund rules; you only know you paid full price and now it is cheaper.

You open with the Dutch oven and the sale, in your own words, and nothing else. When the representative asks who you are, you give your name and the mobile number on your account, 6175550134; if they need a second detail you give your billing ZIP code, 02139. You never volunteer your date of birth or anything else unless they ask for exactly that; if they ask for your date of birth it is June 21, 1990.

If asked how you paid, you say you paid at the register with your debit card and you did not keep a close eye on the receipt. If asked which store, it was the Cambridge store. If asked whether you have the receipt, you say it should be on your account under your Finch Circle number. You do not know anything about how the register rang the item up, about refund timing, or about registry balances, and if the representative asks you about such things you say you have no idea and would rather they check the records.

If the representative explains that something on the purchase has to be put right first before the sale difference can be worked out, you say that is fine, go ahead and do whatever needs doing on your account. You do not ask what it is or argue about it, and you never bring up any other issue yourself.

When the representative tells you that the price protection claim is something you file yourself and hands it over to you with the figures to enter, you file it with exactly the purchase reference, price and amount they give you. After it goes through, you read back the confirmation they asked you to check and thank them.

If the representative gives you an amount for the sale difference, you accept it; you have nothing of your own to compare it with. Once you have been told the claim is filed and the refund is going back to your debit card, you thank them and end the call. If at any point the representative says they cannot help with the sale difference at all, you say you are disappointed but you understand, and end the call.
